# Final quiz {.unnumbered}

Ten questions covering the whole book. Answer them all, then click **Check answers**. The explanations say which chapter to revisit if you get one wrong.

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

**1.** You want the mean height of females only. Which code works?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(webexercises::longmcq(c(
  "`mean(morph$Height, Sex == \"Female\")`",
  answer = "`females <- subset(morph, Sex == \"Female\")`, then `mean(females$Height)`",
  "`females <- subset(morph, Sex = \"Female\")`, then `mean(females$Height)`",
  "`subset(mean(morph$Height), Sex == \"Female\")`"
)))
```

**2.** Which plot is best for comparing height between males and females?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(webexercises::longmcq(c(
  "`hist(morph$Height)`",
  "`plot(Height ~ HandLength, data = morph)`",
  answer = "`boxplot(Height ~ Sex, data = morph)`",
  "A plot is not needed before a t-test"
)))
```

**3.** A study finds a difference of 2 cm (95% CI -1 to 5 cm, p = 0.21). What is the best conclusion?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(webexercises::longmcq(c(
  "There is no difference",
  "The difference is exactly 2 cm",
  "The study shows a large effect",
  answer = "The data fit anything from a 1 cm decrease to a 5 cm increase, so we cannot tell"
)))
```

**4.** Which describes the uncertainty in an estimate, rather than the spread of the data?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(webexercises::longmcq(c(
  answer = "The standard error",
  "The standard deviation",
  "The median",
  "The range"
)))
```

**5.** In `lm(Height ~ HandLength, data = morph)`, which is the response variable?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(webexercises::longmcq(c(
  "HandLength",
  answer = "Height",
  "Both",
  "Neither"
)))
```

**6.** A cricket model gives temperature = 22.8 + 3.41 × chirps (°F). What is the predicted temperature at 10 chirps per second?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(webexercises::longmcq(c(
  "22.8 \u00b0F",
  "34.1 \u00b0F",
  answer = "56.9 \u00b0F",
  "260 \u00b0F"
)))
```

**7.** If you collected a much larger sample, what would most likely happen?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(webexercises::longmcq(c(
  answer = "The confidence intervals would get narrower",
  "The standard deviation would get much smaller",
  "The slope would get bigger",
  "The p-value would get bigger"
)))
```

**8.** You get the error `cannot open file 'data/morphometry.csv': No such file or directory`. What should you check first?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(webexercises::longmcq(c(
  "Reinstall R",
  "Switch to read.csv2()",
  "Restart your computer",

```

**9.** Which is the best write-up of the height result?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(webexercises::longmcq(c(
  "Males were significantly taller than females (p < 0.001)",
  answer = "Males were on average 15.1 cm taller than females (95% CI 13.4 to 16.7 cm; p < 0.001)",
  "p < 0.001, so males are taller",
  "There was a significant difference in height between the sexes"
)))
```

**10.** Why write your code in a script rather than typing it in the Console?

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(webexercises::longmcq(c(
  "Scripts run faster",
  "The Console cannot do statistics",
  "Plots only work from a script",
  answer = "You can run the whole analysis again later and see exactly what you did"
)))
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why? Answers explained

1. == compares; a single = gives an error. subset() keeps the rows, then mean() works on one column. (Chapter 4)
2. A box plot shows a number by group. A histogram has no groups; a scatter plot needs two numbers. (Chapter 5)
3. The confidence interval includes zero but also sizeable effects. A large p-value does not show there is no difference. (Chapter 6 and the Glossary)
4. The SD describes the data; the SE describes how much an estimate would vary between samples. (Glossary)
5. In y ~ x, y is the response. Here height is explained by hand length. (Chapter 7 and the Glossary)
6. 22.8 + 3.41 × 10 = 22.8 + 34.1 = 56.9. (Chapter 7)
7. More data makes estimates more precise, so the standard error and the confidence interval shrink. The SD of the data stays about the same. (Glossary)
8. This error almost always means R is looking in the wrong folder or the file name is misspelt. (Chapters 1 and 3)
9. Give the size of the effect and its confidence interval first. "Significant" alone says nothing about how big the difference is. (Chapter 6)
10. A script is a saved record of your analysis. Code typed in the Console is gone when you close RStudio. (Chapter 2)
:::
